Why ESPN is WRONG about eSports

I have no issue with ESPN airing eSports.

He makes a good point in comparing eSports to things like poker, cupstacking, spelling bees, etc... if you are some kind of ESPN purist... me on the other hand I find it unwatchable garbage 20 hours out of most days... and I'm a pretty vocal sports fan.

Here's some ways that the NBA differs from LoL. The NBA actively fines and punishes cheaters. Performance enhancing drugs are banned. Point shaving is among the gravest offenses that one can commit on a court or field.

None of that seems to matter to eSports... and I don't see anybody mentioning it. All I see are a bunch of people trying to legitimize their corrupt hobby. I'm sure many of these people have cried about the corruption of FIFA while ignoring the fact that there are eSports cases of fixed matches.

You want people like me to take you seriously? Regulate it. Don't allow for "We Are Sorry" teams to exist.

Now the drafting system is not worse than a meritocracy. It is a system based on parity. It makes it so that any team could be any team. In eSports the best players flock to the best teams. It's the same few teams winning every year.

Lots of obvious google misinformation, for example NFL players spend much more than 5-7 hours a day preparing for gamely during the season. Collegiate football players spend about 5-7 hours a day during their season.

Something that he didn't mention is that the easiest way for eSports to make a name for themselves is probably through regular sports. Games like Madden, NBA2k, and FIFA are insanely popular but are currently based around being yearly roster updates. If they instead focused on an eSports oriented experience they would make huge profits. That's my dream anyway, they realize that the roster update refresh method is less profitable than releases a base game that allows the community to just compete and have fun.

So DOTA got more viewers on Twitch (which he calls "inaccesible"?) than game 7 of the 2013 NBA Finals? I'm pretty sure ABC's viewership is only in the US, while the DOTA viewership was worldwide.

And calling something a "meritocracy" doesn't make it better (and the system he calls "better" is only better in individual sports. Which is why it gets used in things like golf and tennis). The draft system (along with the salary cap) ensures that the Patriots don't win the championship every single year. It spreads the talent around the league; would the NFL be very fun to watch if Tom Brady, Peyton Manning, and Aaron Rodgers were all on the same team? I don't think so.

People don't watch tennis because they toss a tennis ball with their dog. People aren't going to watch something because suddenly they're using Xboxes to compete. You don't see people running around wearing football helmets or shoulder pads. They wear the jerseys because they want to support the sport/team, not the other way around. People buy Jordans and Starburys because the athletes advertise them.

Belittling major injuries isn't going to win you any friends. Guys in sports don't break their leg "catching a ball to score imaginary points" usually. They get their legs broken by getting hit by 250 pound linebackers or being unable to cancel your momentum. Whether you think they're the same or not, you'll never convince someone that tearing an ACL or breaking bones is the same as the repetitive use injuries that gamers get in their hands/wrists.

And the 5-7 hour figure might work for high school or college (where the NCAA specifically limits you to 20 hours per week, or they might be required to do more), but in-season NFL players spend way more time practicing, training, watching game film, getting injuries treated, learning game plans, etc.

Also, it might just be me, but I get the general feeling that the whole time he's vaguely insulting people who watch traditional sports.

And yes, World Series of Poker, spelling bee, etc. are often decried by purists as "not belonging on a sports channel". I have a feeling they're the same ones complaining about DOTA.
